In the cosmic and geological sections, time runs from left to right. Each band contains its name in the centre and dates at its ends. Highlighting and small brackets identify the interval enlarged in the next band. Tap an upper band, or use Back, to return to that level.

Subdivisions are named within the timeline. Tap a region or its name to enlarge it. When a region is too narrow, a short line connects its name to its exact position; durations remain proportional. The Solar System and Earth bands show parallel histories within cosmic history. Previous and Next move through divisions of the same rank, including across era boundaries.

The − sign means before today; + means time since the Big Bang. Cosmic chapter boundaries are approximate. Geological divisions follow the international timescale independently of the rounded age of the Universe. Expand the dating notes below the text for details.

The module covers cosmic history, Earth’s four eons, and the three eras and twelve periods of the Phanerozoic. Earlier eons remain broad overviews. A first selection of common ancestors is linked to the tree of life through documented dating ranges. Human history now has %1$d reading windows and %2$d documented landmarks across several continents. This foundation will be expanded, along with finer geological divisions; it is not an exhaustive history.

Original schematic illustrations, drawn in code. They are not photographs or simulations to scale. No image downloads are needed; all entries are available offline. Source links open online.\n\nSources reviewed in October 2026.
NASA / Webb · The lives of stars
ESA / Gaia · The Milky Way’s thick disc
An expanding, cooling Universe, initially extremely hot and dense.
The Big Bang describes the early evolution of space and its contents. It was not an explosion at one location inside pre-existing empty space.
The starting point is a convention. It does not establish what happened at an exact “instant zero”.
A proposed phase in the very earliest instants
A very brief episode of extremely rapid expansion.
Inflation helps explain the Universe’s large-scale uniformity and the seeds of later structures. Its physical mechanism remains unknown.
A theoretical scenario, with no measured start date. Grouped at the origin for navigation; no exact timing is implied.
A few microseconds after the Big Bang
Quarks become bound inside the building blocks of atomic nuclei.
As the primordial plasma cools, quarks and gluons no longer move freely through it. Protons and neutrons form. Ordinary neutral atoms will appear much later.
An order of magnitude. The point represents the first few microseconds, not a single precisely dated event.
Primordial nucleosynthesis produces helium and traces of other light nuclei.

Protons and neutrons combine while the Universe is still hot enough for nuclear reactions. Expansion soon stops this brief episode. Most ordinary matter remains hydrogen, with a substantial helium fraction.
A process lasting minutes. The marker is placed near three minutes; nuclei are not yet neutral atoms.
About 380,000 years after the Big Bang
Neutral atoms form and the primordial light is released.
Electrons bind to nuclei as the gas cools. Photons scatter much less often. This ancient radiation, stretched by expansion, is now observed as the cosmic microwave background.
An approximate age for an extended transition, called recombination. This is not the birth of starlight.
After recombination, before the first stars
Gravity gathers gas while the Universe has no stars yet.
Small density differences grow. Ordinary gas falls into gravitational concentrations dominated by dark matter, preparing the sites where stars and galaxies will emerge.
The marker indicates the beginning. The end is gradual and depends on when the first stars form.
Within the first few hundred million years
Gravity ignites the first stellar furnaces.

Hydrogen and helium clouds collapse until fusion can begin. Their ultraviolet light starts to transform the surrounding gas. These earliest stellar generations are a major target of cosmic-dawn research.
No exact first-star date is known. The point near 200 million years is an illustrative, approximate anchor.
During the first few hundred million years
Stars and gas assemble into young galaxies.
Small systems grow by gathering gas and merging. Their early appearance differs from today’s large spiral galaxies. Observations probe increasingly early stages of this assembly.
There is no single birth date for all galaxies. The point near 300 million years is a navigation landmark, not an earliest-observation record.
From the first stellar generations onward
Stellar evolution supplies material for later stars and rocky planets.

Fusion inside stars produces elements such as carbon and oxygen. Winds and stellar explosions return enriched matter to space. Later generations incorporate it; other processes, including neutron-star mergers, also contribute to heavy-element production.
An ongoing process. Its early marker is schematic, not the date when all chemical elements appeared.
Parts of the thick disc: about 13 billion years old
The Milky Way preserves an ancient record in its stars.
Gaia-based research dates the beginning of thick-disc formation to roughly 0.8 billion years after the Big Bang. Gas accretion, star formation and mergers subsequently reshape our galaxy.
This estimate concerns a component of the Milky Way. It is not a single birth date for the entire galaxy.
Largely complete by about 1 billion years
Early sources of light transform intergalactic hydrogen.

Energetic radiation removes electrons from neutral hydrogen. Ionized regions expand and overlap over hundreds of millions of years, letting ultraviolet light travel farther through intergalactic space.
The marker represents a late stage, not the start. Reionization is gradual and varies from place to place.
Galaxies gather along a vast network of filaments.
Gravity amplifies initial density differences. Dark matter and gas form a network containing galaxies, groups and clusters, separated by more sparsely populated regions. Its growth continues today.
The point near one billion years introduces this long process. It is not a measured birth date of the web.
On average, the Universe forms stars far faster than it does today.
This broad period of intense star formation is sometimes called cosmic noon. Since then, the average rate across the Universe has declined, although individual galaxies follow different histories.
A broad maximum in a cosmic average. It is neither an instantaneous event nor the peak of every galaxy.
The expansion of the Universe enters an accelerating phase.
Gravity previously slowed the expansion. At late times, the component described as dark energy becomes increasingly important. Its physical nature remains unresolved.
An approximate transition inferred within cosmological models. Acceleration is not the beginning of expansion, nor the same date as equal matter and dark-energy densities.
A collapsing cloud gives rise to the Solar System.

Most material gathers at the centre to form the Sun. In the surrounding disc, solids collide and accumulate into larger bodies. The planets take shape over time from material inherited from earlier stellar generations.
An approximate age for the system’s formation. The Sun and all planets did not finish forming simultaneously.

Repeated impacts assemble Earth from smaller bodies. Heating and differentiation separate its interior into layers. Radiometric dating, particularly of meteorites, constrains the age of Earth’s formation.
The estimate is about 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years. Formation took time; the illustration depicts an early hot Earth, not modern continents.
A major impact offers the leading explanation for our satellite.

In giant-impact scenarios, a collision involving the young Earth launches material into orbit. Part of that debris assembles into the Moon. Lunar samples and simulations help reconstruct this early history.
The timing and details remain debated. The marker near 4.5 billion years ago is deliberately approximate.
About 13.8 billion years after the Big Bang
Stars form and die, galaxies evolve, and space continues to expand. Looking farther into space also reveals earlier stages of this history, because light takes time to reach us.
The age is rounded. This endpoint represents the present, not the end of the Universe.

Scientific references for the cosmic and geological timeline. Cosmic chapters use approximate reading boundaries; Earth’s geological divisions follow the international timescale. Dating uncertainties are explained in the entries.
Explore this period on the timeline

From the hot, dense early Universe to the first galaxies: matter cools, neutral atoms form, then stars begin transforming their surroundings. This chapter brings together the primordial Universe, the dark ages and cosmic dawn. Its endpoint near one billion years is an approximate reading boundary, around the late stages of reionization.
From about one billion years after the Big Bang to today

Galaxies grow and change, stars enrich their surroundings, and the cosmic web develops. Across this long chapter, the average rate of star formation reaches a broad maximum and later declines, while expansion eventually accelerates. Galaxies already existed before the beginning of this chapter.
From its formation about 4.6 billion years ago to today

The Sun and planets belong to a much older galactic history. This parallel band begins with their formation and continues to the present. The available entries currently describe the birth of the Sun, Earth and Moon; the band does not imply that their formation lasted until today.
From about 4.54 billion years ago to today

From its formation around 4.54 billion years ago to today, Earth changes into a world of oceans, continents and diverse life. Its four eons provide the first level of exploration. Open the Phanerozoic to discover its three eras, then their geological periods.
From the earliest instants to about 380,000 years

Expansion cools the early Universe. Protons and neutrons form, followed by light nuclei. Much later, electrons bind to nuclei and the primordial light can travel freely. The end of this chapter corresponds approximately to recombination.
From about 380,000 years to the first stars

After recombination, gravity gathers gas into structures, but no stars illuminate the Universe yet. This chapter ends progressively as the first stars appear. The boundary near 200 million years is an approximate navigation landmark, not a precisely measured date.
Roughly 200 million to one billion years after the Big Bang

Stars and young galaxies light up the cosmos. They enrich gas with new elements, and their radiation gradually reionizes intergalactic hydrogen. The boundaries are approximate: these changes unfold at different times in different regions.

Earth assembles through accretion and undergoes major impacts, including the one linked to the Moon’s formation. Its surface gradually cools. Ancient zircons suggest that liquid water was already present during this eon. The surviving geological record is very sparse.

Continental cores grow within a largely oceanic world. Microbial life leaves traces, including some layered structures called stromatolites. These records document ancient life, but do not establish exactly when it began. The atmosphere contains very little free oxygen.

Oxygen accumulates in the atmosphere, transforming oceans and living environments. Cells with nuclei and multicellular organisms diversify over this long interval. Continents repeatedly assemble and separate; severe glaciations occur. Near the end, the Ediacaran biota includes large, soft-bodied organisms.

Abundant animal fossils make this part of Earth’s history especially readable in rocks. Life diversifies in the seas and spreads across the continents, while extinctions reshape ecosystems. This eon includes the Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic, and continues today. Life itself is much older.

Marine animals diversify, plants and arthropods spread on land, and forests and early land vertebrates appear. Continents converge into Pangaea. The era ends with the end-Permian mass extinction, the largest known biodiversity crisis of the Phanerozoic.

Pangaea breaks apart. Dinosaurs diversify on land; other reptiles occupy the seas and skies. Early mammals and birds are also part of this world, and flowering plants spread during the Cretaceous. The final extinction eliminates non-avian dinosaurs; the bird lineage survives.

Mammals and birds diversify after the end-Cretaceous extinction. Over the long term, a changing climate cools and major ice sheets develop. Grasslands expand in many regions. The human lineage appears very late in this era, which is still ongoing.

Animal forms diversify rapidly in the oceans during the Cambrian radiation. Trilobites, sponges and many other groups inhabit marine environments. Hard parts become common in the fossil record. This diversification unfolds over millions of years: it is neither instantaneous nor the origin of life.

Marine biodiversity expands considerably, with brachiopods, bryozoans and cephalopods among the abundant groups. Near the end, glaciation and major sea-level changes accompany a mass extinction that severely affects life in the oceans.

Marine ecosystems recover after the end-Ordovician extinction. Reefs expand and jawed fishes diversify. Small vascular plants and terrestrial arthropods testify to the development of land ecosystems, still very different from later forests.

Fishes become highly diverse, while the first forests transform continental environments. Early tetrapods evolve within the lobe-finned vertebrate lineage and retain strong ties to water. Repeated biodiversity crises in the Late Devonian particularly affect marine ecosystems.

Extensive swamp forests in equatorial regions accumulate plant material that will form major coal deposits. Amphibians and insects diversify, and early amniotes can reproduce away from open water. These forests do not cover the entire planet: other regions experience different environments, including glaciation.

Pangaea dominates the continental arrangement, with extensive dry interiors. Reptiles and synapsids diversify on land; synapsids include the lineage that will give rise to mammals. The period ends with a mass extinction that profoundly disrupts both marine and terrestrial ecosystems.

Ecosystems rebuild after the end-Permian crisis. Early dinosaurs, pterosaurs and mammalian relatives diversify. Pangaea begins to fracture. A further mass extinction closes the period, after which dinosaurs become particularly prominent in terrestrial ecosystems.

The fragmentation of Pangaea continues. Sauropods and theropod dinosaurs diversify among landscapes rich in gymnosperms, including conifers. Early birds are known from this period: they belong to the theropod dinosaur lineage. Marine reptiles occupy the oceans, but are not dinosaurs.

Flowering plants spread and diversify while dinosaurs remain prominent on land. Continents continue to separate and extensive shallow seas develop. At the end, the Chicxulub asteroid impact triggers a global crisis: non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites disappear, while birds and many other lineages survive.

Mammals diversify into many ecological roles after the end-Cretaceous extinction. Early representatives of numerous living groups appear, including whales. A generally warm early climate gives way to substantial cooling later in the period, with major Antarctic glaciation near the start of the Oligocene.

Grasslands expand in many regions and herbivore communities change. Climate and ocean circulation evolve as continents approach their current arrangement. Apes diversify; early members of the human lineage appear in Africa. Their history is a branching evolution, not a straight progression towards modern humans.

Repeated glacial and interglacial cycles reshape landscapes and sea levels. Several human species live during this period; Homo sapiens emerges and spreads widely. The Quaternary comprises the Pleistocene and Holocene and continues today. Human prehistory and written history occupy only its most recent portion.

Ma means millions of years before the present. Numerical ages may be revised; a value without ± is not necessarily exact. Most Phanerozoic boundaries are defined by reference levels in rock sequences. Environmental changes need not occur simultaneously everywhere.

The band starts at Earth’s estimated age: 4,540 ± 50 Ma. The formal Hadean starts at 4,567 Ma in the geological timescale, near the beginning of the Solar System; only the part within Earth’s history is shown here.
This view currently stops at the major geological divisions. Finer subdivisions and dated events will be added progressively.
Earth’s history is organised into eons, then eras and periods. The first three eons together form the Precambrian. The Phanerozoic occupies only about 12% of Earth’s history.
NASA · Ancient zircons and early oceans

Geological boundaries and their uncertainties follow the June 2026 ICS chart. NPS articles support the explanations of environments and life; their older numerical boundaries are not used here. The Hadean is clipped to Earth’s estimated age. Geological colours use an original palette, not the official chart colours.
From the Big Bang to 25 minutes
As the very hot Universe cools, particles and then light nuclei form. This chapter covers the first 25 minutes; its milestones describe processes, some still hypothetical, rather than exact instants.

A history spanning 13.8 billion years, from the first moments to today’s galaxies. The Sun and Earth appear much later in this story.

The observable Universe was once extremely hot and dense. As it expands, it cools, allowing light nuclei and then atoms to form. Gravity gradually gathers matter into the structures where stars and galaxies develop.
Galaxies continue evolving while new planetary systems form. Earth’s history unfolds within cosmic history. The Solar System and Earth links let you explore this smaller scale.
A cloud of gas and dust gives rise to the Sun and a disc of material. Bodies gradually assemble within that disc, forming the future planets.

Gravity draws matter together, and the Sun holds most of the system’s mass. Dust and small bodies collide around it. Conditions vary with distance from the star, contributing to the diversity of planets and smaller objects.

Planets continue changing after formation. Collisions, internal cooling and interactions with their surroundings transform their surfaces and atmospheres. Earth provides a distinctive journey through geology, climate and life.
Earth changed dramatically long before familiar animals appeared. Oceans, continents, atmosphere and life evolve together through four eons.

Earth forms as material in the young Solar System accumulates. As it cools, it develops a solid crust. Movement within its interior, volcanism, erosion and tectonics then continually reshape its surface.
Most of the story is microscopic

For an immense span of time, life is mainly microbial. The Precambrian groups the Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic. Despite its rich animal fossil record, the Phanerozoic occupies only about 12% of Earth’s history. The four bands let you compare these durations without making them artificially equal.
The rocks of this eon preserve an abundant history of animals. Across three eras, from ancient seas to modern landscapes, ecosystems diversify and recover from major crises.

During the Paleozoic, marine animals diversify and plants and animals spread across land. The Mesozoic includes the expansion of dinosaurs and the fragmentation of Pangaea. During the Cenozoic, mammals and birds occupy a wide variety of environments.

Abundant fossils do not mean that life begins here: it existed long before. Shells, skeletons and traces of activity help scientists compare rocks. These records remain incomplete, and some organisms and environments are preserved much better than others.
Pangaea breaks apart, new oceans open and ecosystems reorganize. The Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous tell three distinct parts of this long transformation.
A world of land and sea

The gradual separation of continents alters coastlines, ocean circulation and the routes along which organisms can disperse. Shallow seas cover extensive regions. Landscapes differ from place to place and change throughout the era.

Dinosaurs occupy many terrestrial environments. Oceans contain ammonites and large marine reptiles, while pterosaurs fly overhead. Mammals and birds also form part of this world. Flowering plants diversify in the Cretaceous. At the end of that period, non-avian dinosaurs disappear, while birds survive.
From conifer forests to seas inhabited by ammonites, the Jurassic contains varied ecosystems. Large sauropods and many theropods diversify.

Pangaea continues to fragment. Moving continents transform seas and terrestrial habitats. Gymnosperms, including conifers, are prominent in the vegetation. These landscapes differ from today’s flower-filled grasslands.

Fossils such as Archaeopteryx document early birds during the Jurassic. They belong to the theropod dinosaur lineage. Pterosaurs, which also fly, form a different group; marine reptiles are not dinosaurs either.

A geological period does not necessarily begin and end with extinctions. Its boundaries help scientists correlate sequences of rocks. The numerical ages used to place them on the timeline are estimates that can be refined.

The highlighted interval locates an estimate for the last common ancestor of this group’s living members. Its width represents uncertainty in the dating, not how long the group existed. It does not date the first fossil or the appearance of every characteristic shared by these organisms.

This molecular-clock study gives a composite range of 4.52–3.94 billion years across its sensitivity analyses. LUCA is the last common ancestor of cellular life alive today, not the first life on Earth. This very ancient estimate depends strongly on the dating assumptions.

A molecular-clock study places the diversification of the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) between 1.80 and 1.67 billion years ago. The evolution leading to that ancestor began earlier. This is a published model-based estimate, not a boundary fixed for all studies.

This range comes from the composite columns of a molecular-clock study: an envelope of 95% intervals from selected analyses. It excludes some of the paper’s alternative calibration strategies and tree topologies. Fossil calibrations and model choices affect the result; it is not the full range of every published estimate.

The range combines the 95% dating intervals across the tree topologies tested in a molecular-clock study. It concerns the common ancestor of living land plants, not the first organism ever to live on land. Fossils constrain the estimate without directly identifying this ancestor.

The 8–6 million-year range is an approximate synthesis for the common ancestor of the human and chimpanzee lineages, not a statistical confidence interval. This ancestor was neither a modern human nor a modern chimpanzee. The estimate does not date the origin of Homo sapiens.

No age is inferred from the number or length of branches. LUCA uses the study’s wider sensitivity envelope; animal ages use Table 1 composite ranges, excluding calibration strategies 3 and 4 and alternative topologies. Land-plant ranges combine the tested topologies. The human–chimpanzee estimate is a general synthesis, not a statistical interval. These ranges have different meanings and should not be compared as equal confidence levels. Each dating window states its limitations. Numerical precision reproduces the source and does not imply accuracy to the last decimal. Previous and Next browse records ordered by the older end of each range; this order is not an evolutionary lineage. The branching symbol is schematic and does not reconstruct the ancestor.
